laintiff Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission” or the “SEC”) files

SUMMARY 
1. This case involves a global, crypto asset-related, multi-level marketing pyramid
and Ponzi scheme that raised over $1.7 billion from victims worldwide, including millions from 
U.S. investors.  Defendants and others operated the scheme through a series of projects referred

2. The HyperTech Group, a purported blockchain technology conglomerate  
founded by Lee and others (collectively, the “Founders”) launched HyperFund in June 2020.  At 
the outset, HyperFund claimed to be a project dedicated to creating a so-called “decentralized 
finance (DeFi) ecosystem” for crypto asset market participants.  Over time, the project’s stated 
goals evolved and utilized various names in an effort to capitalize on the buzz words and 
zeitgeist of the day, including rebranding itself as “HyperVerse” and, later, as “HyperNation,” a 
version of the project which featured an individual in a mask discussing creating a decentralized 
government to escape the societal bonds of inequality and injustice through blockchain 
technology.  HyperFund, including its subsequent rebranded iterations, is now defunct.   
3. From June 2020 through May 2022, HyperFund offered so-called “membership” 
packages promising exorbitant passive returns, supposedly derived in part from HyperFund’s 
crypto asset mining operations.  For example, HyperFund promised returns of 0.5% to 1% per 
day, with the prospect of tripling ones’ initial investment in 600 days.  HyperFund also 
implemented a pyramid scheme-like referral system to reward existing members for recruiting 
new investors.   
4. HyperFund’s membership packages were offered and sold as investment  
contracts, and therefore, securities under the federal securities laws, because investors made an 
investment of money in a common enterprise with a reasonable expectation of profits from the 
efforts of Defendants or third parties.  The membership packages were offered and sold without 
registration, and without qualifying for any exemption from registration. 
5. Lee was centrally involved with HyperFund throughout its lifecycle.  Lee was a 
co-founder of HyperTech Group, which claimed to be involved in “Large Scale Crypto Mining,” 
including bitcoin, that promoters asserted was a key revenue source for HyperFund.  However, 
Case 1:24-cv-00296-RDB   Document 1   Filed 01/29/24   Page 2 of 31

Lee later admitted that HyperTech Group was not engaged in large-scale bitcoin mining.  Lee 
was also featured prominently during HyperVerse’s launch event, and he even claimed to be 
helping to resurrect HyperVerse after its collapse, as a way of recouping investor losses.   
6. Chunga (known online by her nickname “Bitcoin Beautee”) was one of 
HyperFund’s top promoters and arguably the face of its United States presence.  Chunga’s 
recruitment efforts through online seminars and videos included the typical promotional ruses 
associated with fraudulent multi-level marketing schemes.  Here, that included focusing on 
investors’ supposed ability to make money via daily passive rewards, and also via so-called 
“accelerated” rewards if investors convinced others to join.  Chunga’s pitch was successful.  
Within six months, Chunga earned the highest level a HyperFund promoter could achieve, 
which, according to promotional materials, required at least $5 million in new investments, 
which were referred to as “sales,” and she continued to generate additional new investments long 
after that.  Chunga received over $3.7 million, both from the platform and directly from 
investors.  She used her earnings to fund extravagant personal expenses and help recruit others 
into the scheme by showing off the potential wealth to be earned through HyperFund.   
7. HyperFund, however, was a pyramid and Ponzi scheme.  HyperFund had no  
real source of revenue other than funds received from investors, and Defendants had no basis for 
the promised returns.  HyperFund did not engage in large-scale crypto asset mining, despite the 
claims by promoters like Chunga that the investors’ passive rewards were being paid by such 
efforts.  HyperFund even hired an actor to pretend to be the new CEO when HyperVerse was 
launched.  With no apparent legitimate source of revenues, investor withdrawals were paid with 
new investor deposits.    
Case 1:24-cv-00296-RDB   Document 1   Filed 01/29/24   Page 3 of 31

8. Chunga ignored red flags about HyperFund and made several misrepresentations  
to investors to convince them to join.  Lee knew or recklessly disregarded that the presentations 
used by the promoters, like Chunga, included false statements.  Lee also made statements to 
investors that were misleading by omitting material information about the nature of the business.  
Ultimately, the scheme collapsed in 2022 when investors were no longer able to make 
withdrawals.   
9. From approximately June 2020 to approximately November 2022, Defendants (1) 
raised millions of dollars from retail investors in the United States, and several other countries, 
through the unregistered offer and sale of securities styled as membership interests in 
HyperFund; and (2) made materially false and misleading statements about the investments and 
knowingly or recklessly engaged in a scheme to defraud investors—bilking the investors out of 
over $1.7 billion—by enticing them with the false promise of guaranteed, high returns from 
investments in securities. 
JURISDICTION AND VENUE 
10. The Court has subject matter jurisdiction over this action pursuant to Sections 
20(b), 20(d), and 22(a) of the Securities Act, 15 U.S.C. §§ 77t(b), 77t(d), and 77v(a); and

15. Brenda Indah Chunga a/k/a/ “Bitcoin Beautee,” age 43, resided in Severna  
Park, Maryland during the relevant period.  Chunga has never been associated with a registered 
entity and has no disciplinary history with the Commission.

Group launched HyperFund.  HyperTech Group was featured in presentations as the business 
experience and expertise behind the project to give HyperFund credibility for prospective 
investors and was advertised as the alleged source of the rewards investors earned.   
17. HyperFund is the name of the multi-level marketing project launched by  
HyperTech Group in June 2020 that claimed to be building a so-called decentralized finance 
ecosystem.  HyperFund was subsequently rebranded to HyperVerse in or about December 2021, 
and then rebranded to HyperNation in or about May 2022.     
FACTS 
A. Chunga and Lee Offered and Sold Securities Through HyperFund 
The Global Launch of HyperFund 
18. On June 11, 2020, in a press release issued through a paid service, the  
HyperTech Group announced that it was launching HyperFund.  The press release billed 
HyperFund as an “upgrade of HyperCapital,” a similar multi-level marketing project one of 
HyperFund’s Founders attempted to launch six months earlier, in January 2020.   
19. The press release described Lee as the founder and Chairman of HyperFund and  
listed Lee as the “contact” for inquiries.  
20. In the press release, Lee was quoted as saying that the upgrade reflected a change  
in the strategic focus and development plans of the company.  The press release claimed 
HyperFund would be “more streamlined and better equipped to handle the challenges and 
opportunities in the traditional finance and cryptocurrency market” and would have three key 
focus areas: tech incubation, investment and funding, and community building. 
Case 1:24-cv-00296-RDB   Document 1   Filed 01/29/24   Page 6 of 31
7 
 
21. The press release also claimed that HyperTech Group planned to be listed on the 
Hong Kong Stock Exchange by 2022 and that it intended to launch products such as HyperNews, 
HyperTalk, and HyperShow, supposedly blockchain-based social networking platforms.      
22. The presentations Chunga later used to recruit investors similarly prominently 
featured these and other details about the Founders, including Lee, and the entities that 
purportedly comprised the HyperFund Group on slides that were labeled “Credibility,” including 
slides featuring screenshots of Lee appearing on CNN and other media outlets.  One of the 
details Chunga touted was the fact that Lee and another one of the Founders were featured and 
interviewed in an episode of an Amazon Prime documentary series called “Next: Blockchain.”      
23. In one presentation, Chunga leveraged HyperFund’s Founders’ public-facing  
profiles in order to persuade investors that there was no risk in investing with the HyperTech 
Group:  
Some people say things, how do we know they won’t just take our money and 
disappear?  Well, ladies and gents, they have more to lose than to gain. They’re 
all over CNN.  They have publicly traded companies, they are on Amazon Prime, 
their faces are everywhere.  They have more to lose than to gain.   
 
24. As Chunga emphasized in other presentations: “[L]adies and gents, this is not a  
company that needs your money. . . .  He doesn’t need us.”  (emphasis added).   
25. On information and belief, Lee was not only a co-founder of HyperFund, but he  
maintained control over HyperFund throughout its existence.  Lee’s background and role as co-
founder of HyperFund was a prominent feature of the marketing and promotional materials used 
by promoters to attract new investors.  Lee was aware or recklessly disregarded that 
HyperFunds’s marketing materials used to recruit investors contained material misstatements 
because he admitted as much during a call with an investor.  Lee also recorded a message that 
was released as part of the launch of HyperVerse in December 2021, and later appeared in video-
Case 1:24-cv-00296-RDB   Document 1   Filed 01/29/24   Page 7 of 31
8 
 
teleconference calls with promoters and others to attempt to assuage the concerns of 
HyperFund’s investors.  
HyperFund’s “Membership Rewards” Program 
26. Investors purchased “memberships” in HyperFund at various levels using the 
crypto asset Tether (USDT).  For example, in her HyperFund videos, Chunga encouraged 
investors to “Choose Your Membership” level:  $300, $500, $1,000, or $10,000.  Typically 
HyperFund promoters, including Chunga, gave a link to investors through which the investors 
would use Tether to purchase the package.  On the HyperFund platform, the value of the 
individual’s membership level was reflected in the form of an internal value called HyperUnits, 
or HU.  For example, a $300 membership was reflected as 300 HyperUnits.   
27. Chunga told investors who purchased a membership that they would receive:  (1)  
access to a crypto asset educational platform; (2) exclusive pre-sale offerings of future crypto 
asset projects, such as, initial coin offerings (“ICOs”) at 20%-30% below market value; and (3) 
automatic returns on their investment, which were called “rewards.”  
28. HyperFund offered two ways for members to make money:  passive rewards, 
which promised investors a daily return of 0.5% to 1% of the value of their investment until they 
earned triple the value of their initial investment, and leveraged or accelerated rewards.     
29. As Chunga explained in a promotional video recorded on or about February 9, 
2021, “[Y]ou will receive your initial membership in 6.5 months, lets round it up to 7 months. . .   
You now have your initial investment amount back in your pocket.  And then what happens after 
that?  Everything else that’s coming to you every day after that, what is that?  That is pure profit.  
You did not have to work for it.”  
Case 1:24-cv-00296-RDB   Document 1   Filed 01/29/24   Page 8 of 31
9 
 
30. According to Chunga, “here, with HyperFund, your money is doing all of the 
work for you and you don’t even have to get out of bed.”   
31. Investors could supposedly also earn “accelerated” rewards by recruiting new 
investors which promoters, like Chunga, encouraged HyperFund investors to do.   
32. HyperFund offered three types of leveraged rewards:  Community Rewards, VIP  
Rewards, and Global Rewards.  First, with respect to Community Rewards, Chunga explained in 
her presentations that, in exchange for building the community by referring HyperFund to friends 
and family, HyperFund would supposedly pay investors 20% of their downline’s membership 
value every day up to 20 levels.  HyperFund’s “COMMUNITY REWARD” program was 
detailed in this illustration from a presentation recorded on or about March 9, 2021 and posted to

As Chunga explained: 
The company says in your team, in your group, if you guys have $50,000 in 
membership sales outside of your largest team, we’re going to give you an 
additional half-a-percent every single day on top of everything else they’ve been 
giving you.  They also said, if you make it to Pro, which is $100,000 in 
membership in your entire team, they are going to now pay you an additional one

percent every single day through infinity . . . of your entire organization minus 
your largest leg. 
 
34. HyperFund’s VIP Rewards Program is illustrated in this presentation recorded on  
or about February 9, 2021 and posted on YouTube: 
 
35. Third, highly successful recruiters also supposedly qualified for Global Rewards, 
which were to be paid monthly.  HyperFund claimed that under the Global Rewards program, 
HyperFund took 4% of all company sales—in other words, pooled the funds—and divided them 
among its top promoters.  As a “VIP 5 STAR,” which is the highest level a promoter could 
achieve, Chunga qualified for Global Rewards. 
36. Chunga frequently encouraged investors to increase their membership value by 
reinvesting their rewards through so-called “rebuys” instead of withdrawing them, including in 
the March 9, 2021 presentation recorded and posted on YouTube.   
  
Case 1:24-cv-00296-RDB   Document 1   Filed 01/29/24   Page 10 of 31

37. HyperFund’s structure further discouraged withdrawals.  The only way to  
withdraw the rewards was to convert the internal HyperUnits to so-called “Molecular Future” 
(MOF)—a crypto asset issued, in part, by another founder of HyperFund (“Founder B”)—and 
then transfer the MOF from the HyperFund platform to the HOO Exchange, which was a digital 
asset platform also purportedly owned by Founder B of HyperFund.  From there, the investor 
would need to convert MOF to other crypto assets and transfer them out of the HOO Exchange 
in order to exchange them for fiat currency. 
38. Although the so-called HyperUnits were reflected on the HyperFund platform as   
being pegged at $1 when an investor deposited money (e.g., a $300 membership was equal to 
300 HyperUnits), that was not the case when the HyperUnits were withdrawn after being 
converted to MOF.  In other words, the conversion of HyperUnits to MOF was not pegged $1

# Final OSINT Report: HyperFund / HyperVerse Alleged Crypto Fraud Network

## Executive summary

The benchmark evidence describes HyperFund and its successor brands—HyperVerse and HyperNation—as an alleged global cryptocurrency investment fraud network that combined:

1. **A pyramid/MLM recruitment structure** based on referral commissions and downlines.
2. **Ponzi-like economics**, allegedly promising very high daily returns without a legitimate revenue source.
3. **Public-facing promoters**, particularly Brenda Chunga, who marketed passive income, referral rewards, and apparent wealth.
4. **Repeated rebranding**, from HyperFund to HyperVerse and then HyperNation, while the underlying ecosystem allegedly continued.
5. **Credibility signaling**, including references to founders’ media exposure, corporate affiliations, blockchain expertise, and celebrity endorsements.
6. **A questionable CEO persona**, Steven Reece Lewis, whose claimed education and employment history could not be independently verified by the Guardian.
7. **Withdrawal restrictions and internal-token mechanics**, allegedly making it difficult for investors to convert nominal balances into usable funds.

The SEC complaint alleges that the network raised more than **$1.7 billion**, while DOJ materials and CNBC described the alleged criminal scheme as approximately **$1.89–$1.9 billion**. These figures should be treated as allegations or reported estimates, not as an adjudicated finding in this report. [SRC-004] [SRC-001] [SRC-002]

The DOJ expressly states that criminal charges are allegations and that defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty. [SRC-002]

---

## 1. Network identity and chronology

### HyperFund’s stated structure

The SEC complaint alleges that HyperTech Group launched HyperFund in June 2020 as a purported decentralized-finance ecosystem. HyperFund was later rebranded as HyperVerse around December 2021 and as HyperNation around May 2022. [SRC-004]

The DOJ identifies HyperFund as also being known as HyperTech, HyperCapital, HyperVerse, and HyperNation. [SRC-002] CNBC likewise reports that the project operated under these names. [SRC-001]

### Rebranding sequence

The evidence supports the following sequence:

- **HyperCapital**: identified as an earlier related project or name. [SRC-004] [SRC-002]
- **HyperFund**: launched in June 2020. [SRC-004]
- **HyperVerse**: rebranding around December 2021. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]
- **HyperNation**: rebranding or successor branding around May 2022. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

The SEC complaint alleges that these were successive iterations of the same project ecosystem. The Guardian reports that a senior promoter described HyperVerse and HyperNation as “one big entity,” although this characterization came from the promoter and should not be treated as an independently established corporate fact. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

---

## 2. Alleged investment and Ponzi mechanics

### Promised returns

According to the SEC complaint and DOJ case materials, HyperFund memberships allegedly promised passive returns of approximately **0.5% to 1% per day**, with investors told that their initial investment could double or triple. [SRC-004] [SRC-002]

The Guardian reports that HyperVerse memberships promised a **300% return over 600 days**, with a minimum membership amount of approximately **$300**. [SRC-003]

These promised returns were presented as arising at least partly from cryptocurrency mining operations. However, the SEC alleges that HyperFund had no legitimate revenue source and did not conduct the claimed large-scale mining. [SRC-004] The DOJ similarly alleges that the mining operations used to justify the returns did not exist. [SRC-001] [SRC-002]

### Alleged Ponzi operation

The SEC complaint characterizes HyperFund as both a pyramid and Ponzi scheme. It alleges that:

- There was no apparent legitimate source of revenue.
- The promised returns lacked a valid economic basis.
- Investor withdrawals were paid using deposits from newer investors.
- The scheme collapsed when withdrawals became unavailable. [SRC-004]

The DOJ alleges that investor withdrawals began to be blocked in or around July 2021, while the SEC complaint describes the broader collapse as occurring in 2022. [SRC-001] [SRC-002] [SRC-004]

This is consistent with a possible liquidity-driven failure: high promised returns created continuing obligations, while recruitment and new deposits were needed to sustain the system. That is an assessment based on the alleged mechanics, not an independent finding of fact.

### Internal accounting and withdrawal friction

The SEC complaint alleges that investors purchased memberships using Tether/USDT and received an internal balance denominated in **HyperUnits**. Withdrawals allegedly required conversion of HyperUnits into the MOF crypto asset and movement through the HOO Exchange before conversion into other assets or fiat currency. [SRC-004]

The complaint further alleges that HyperUnits appeared to be valued at $1 when deposited but were not necessarily convertible at that value on withdrawal. It states that MOF’s price had fallen to a very low level by September 2023. [SRC-004]

This structure could have served two functions:

- Making advertised account balances appear stable or dollar-denominated.
- Introducing conversion steps, market-price exposure, and friction that made withdrawals more difficult or less valuable.

That interpretation is an assessment of the reported mechanism; the source does not by itself establish that every investor experienced the same loss or withdrawal outcome.

---

## 3. Recruitment and MLM mechanics

### Referral-based compensation

The SEC alleges that HyperFund used a pyramid-style referral system to reward existing members for recruiting new investors. [SRC-004]

Reported mechanisms included:

- Referral commissions for bringing in new members.
- Additional rewards based on the activity of recruits’ recruits.
- Downline payments extending to as many as 20 levels.
- Community, VIP, and global rewards for successful recruiters. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

The Guardian describes a sliding-scale referral system and commissions based on recruitment down to 20 levels. [SRC-003]

This structure aligned the financial interests of existing members with continued recruitment. It also gave promoters a reason to emphasize recruitment and reinvestment rather than withdrawals.

### Reinvestment incentives

The SEC complaint alleges that promoters encouraged investors to reinvest rewards through “rebuys” instead of withdrawing them. [SRC-004]

The Guardian similarly reports that members were encouraged to reinvest earnings and receive additional HyperUnits when funds were not withdrawn. [SRC-003]

This could have reduced immediate withdrawal pressure and helped retain nominal balances within the platform. It also potentially made the scheme appear to grow through account balances even when funds were not readily accessible.

### Promoter incentives and apparent wealth

Brenda Chunga, also known as “Bitcoin Beautee,” was identified by the SEC as one of HyperFund’s top promoters and a major figure in its U.S. promotional activity. [SRC-004]

The SEC alleges that:

- Chunga reached the highest promoter level within six months.
- That level reportedly required at least $5 million in new referred investments.
- She received more than $3.7 million from the platform and investors.
- She used earnings for extravagant personal expenses and to help recruit others by displaying the apparent wealth available through HyperFund. [SRC-004]

CNBC also reports that the SEC complaint said Chunga received more than $3.7 million and used her earnings to fund personal expenses and recruitment efforts. [SRC-001]

This illustrates a classic social-proof mechanism: visible promoter success can make extraordinary returns appear credible and can shift recruitment from an abstract investment proposition into an aspirational lifestyle pitch.

---

## 4. Public promoters and credibility signaling

### Brenda Chunga / “Bitcoin Beautee”

Chunga allegedly promoted the investment through online seminars and videos. The SEC complaint says her presentations emphasized:

- Daily passive rewards.
- The ability to earn without working.
- Accelerated rewards from recruiting others.
- The supposed credibility of the founders and related companies. [SRC-004]

Her messaging allegedly framed the investment as low-risk because the founders were publicly visible and supposedly had more to lose than gain by misappropriating investor funds. [SRC-004]

This was a credibility-transfer strategy: the apparent reputation of founders, companies, media appearances, and public profiles was used to reassure prospective investors about the safety of the platform.

### Rodney Burton / “Bitcoin Rodney”

The DOJ and CNBC identify Rodney Burton, also known as “Bitcoin Rodney,” as another HyperFund promoter. [SRC-001] [SRC-002]

The available benchmark material establishes his alleged promotional role and criminal charges, but does not provide comparable detail about his specific scripts, recruitment volume, or compensation. Those details remain uncertain on the present evidence.

### Celebrity messages

The Guardian reports that HyperVerse released promotional messages from:

- Steve Wozniak.
- Chuck Norris.
- Jim Norton.
- Lance Bass. [SRC-003]

The messages encouraged support for HyperVerse or its CEO and urged people to join. The Guardian notes that these individuals were available for hire through Cameo and that it was unclear how the messages were obtained. [SRC-003]

The Guardian also states that there was **no suggestion that these celebrities knew the details of HyperVerse’s business model**, and that their messages did not refer to money or investments. [SRC-003]

Accordingly, the evidence supports treating the celebrity appearances as **promotional credibility signals**, not as proof that the celebrities knowingly participated in fraud.

---

## 5. Rebranding as a continuity and repositioning mechanism

The rebranding pattern allowed the project to move through changing narratives:

- HyperFund was presented as a decentralized-finance and crypto investment ecosystem.
- HyperVerse was presented as a metaverse or virtual-world project.
- HyperNation used language involving decentralization, autonomy, a “new world order,” and universal basic income. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

The SEC complaint alleges that the changing names and themes were used to capitalize on contemporary buzzwords and market narratives. [SRC-004]

The Guardian reports that when HyperVerse members experienced withdrawal problems, some were encouraged to migrate to HyperNation. [SRC-003]

This suggests a potential reputational-reset mechanism: when one brand became associated with withdrawal problems or investor dissatisfaction, a new name and more expansive ideological narrative could be used to preserve recruitment momentum. This is an assessment inferred from the chronology and reported migration, not a proven statement of intent.

The evidence does not establish that every legal entity, operator, or participant behind each brand was identical. The SEC and DOJ treat the names as related project iterations, while the Guardian reports a promoter’s description of them as one entity. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-003]

---

## 6. The questionable CEO persona

### Presentation as CEO

The Guardian reports that Steven Reece Lewis was introduced as HyperVerse’s CEO during a December 2021 global launch event. Promotional material described him as:

- A University of Leeds graduate.
- A holder of a master’s degree from Cambridge.
- A former Goldman Sachs employee.
- The seller of a web-development company to Adobe.
- The founder of an IT start-up. [SRC-003]

The launch video reportedly presented him as a qualified executive recruited by HyperTech Group.

### Verification problems

The Guardian states that it found:

- No record of Steven Reece Lewis at the University of Leeds or University of Cambridge.
- No record under that name in UK Companies House records.
- No record at the U.S. SEC.
- No Adobe public filing showing acquisition of a company owned by him.
- No confirmation of employment at Goldman Sachs.
- No LinkedIn profile or meaningful internet presence outside HyperVerse promotional materials. [SRC-003]

The Guardian also reports that a Twitter account in his name was created shortly before the launch, promoted HyperVerse for approximately six months, and then became inactive. [SRC-003]

These findings do not independently prove that the person shown in the launch video was fictitious, nor do they establish who he actually was. They do establish that the claimed biography could not be corroborated by the organizations and public records checked by the Guardian.

### SEC allegation of an actor

The SEC complaint goes further, alleging that HyperFund “hired an actor to pretend to be the new CEO” when HyperVerse launched. [SRC-004]

That is an allegation in a civil complaint, not an adjudicated fact in this report. The Guardian’s inability to verify the stated credentials is consistent with the SEC’s allegation but does not independently prove it.

### Masked successor personas

The Guardian reports that Steven Reece Lewis did not appear in the HyperNation launch video. Instead, masked figures called “Mr H” and “Miss N” were presented as official ambassadors. [SRC-003]

“Mr H” reportedly described himself as an “evangelist in the new world order,” while the presentation promoted decentralization, autonomy, and universal basic income. [SRC-003]

The progression from a credentialed-looking CEO to masked ambassadors may have reduced accountability and made the brand more persona-driven than institution-driven. This is an assessment based on the reported presentations.

---

## 7. Central figures and legal status

### Sam Lee

The SEC complaint identifies Xue Samuel Lee, also known as Sam Lee, as a co-founder and central figure in HyperFund. It alleges that he maintained control throughout the project’s lifecycle and was prominently featured in promotional materials. [SRC-004]

The DOJ charged Lee with conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud in connection with the alleged scheme. [SRC-001] [SRC-002]

Lee denied that HyperVerse was a scam and disputed being its founder, according to the Guardian. [SRC-003] The SEC complaint, however, alleges that he co-founded and controlled HyperFund. [SRC-004]

### Brenda Chunga

Chunga, also known as Bitcoin Beautee, was identified as a top promoter. The DOJ reports that she pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud. [SRC-001] [SRC-002]

### Rodney Burton

Burton, also known as Bitcoin Rodney, was identified as a HyperFund promoter and was charged with offenses relating to an alleged unlicensed money-transmitting business. [SRC-001] [SRC-002]

The DOJ’s case page states that criminal charges are allegations and that defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty. [SRC-002]

---

## 8. Integrated assessment: how the recruitment system functioned

Based only on the benchmark evidence, the alleged system can be modeled as a reinforcing loop:

1. **Attractive promise**: memberships offered extraordinary passive daily returns. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]
2. **Technical justification**: returns were attributed to cryptocurrency mining and blockchain-related operations. [SRC-001] [SRC-002] [SRC-004]
3. **Social proof**: founders’ public profiles, media appearances, corporate claims, celebrity messages, and a purported CEO were used to establish legitimacy. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]
4. **Recruitment incentives**: members could earn additional rewards by recruiting others and building multilevel downlines. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]
5. **Reinvestment**: members were encouraged to leave rewards inside the system and purchase additional nominal units. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]
6. **Withdrawal friction**: conversion through HyperUnits, MOF, and HOO Exchange created additional complexity and possible value loss. [SRC-004]
7. **Brand reset**: when the platform encountered withdrawal problems, the project moved through HyperVerse and HyperNation branding. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]
8. **Liquidity failure**: according to the allegations, withdrawals were blocked and the system collapsed when it could no longer sustain investor demands. [SRC-001] [SRC-002] [SRC-004]

The overall assessment is that the alleged scheme combined the economic characteristics of a **high-return investment fraud** with the social distribution methods of a **multilevel marketing pyramid**, while using rebranding and credibility theater to preserve investor confidence.

---

## 9. Contradictions and unresolved issues

### Contradiction 1: Lee’s role

- The SEC alleges that Lee co-founded and centrally controlled HyperFund. [SRC-004]
- Lee denied that HyperVerse was a scam and disputed being its founder. [SRC-003]

This remains unresolved in the benchmark evidence.

### Contradiction 2: CEO authenticity

- HyperVerse presented Steven Reece Lewis as CEO with an extensive biography. [SRC-003]
- The Guardian found no corroborating records for the claimed qualifications or career history. [SRC-003]
- The SEC alleges that an actor was hired to pretend to be the new CEO. [SRC-004]

The actor allegation remains unproven in this report.

### Contradiction 3: Reported loss or fraud totals

- The SEC complaint alleges more than $1.7 billion raised. [SRC-004]
- DOJ/CNBC materials describe approximately $1.89–$1.9 billion. [SRC-001] [SRC-002]
- The Guardian cites a Chainalysis estimate of approximately $1.3 billion in consumer losses during 2022. [SRC-003]

These figures may refer to different measures—funds raised, alleged fraud amount, or estimated consumer losses—and should not be treated as directly interchangeable.

### Contradiction 4: HyperFund versus HyperNation continuity

- The SEC and DOJ identify HyperVerse and HyperNation as names associated with the same alleged network. [SRC-002] [SRC-004]
- Lee reportedly denied involvement in HyperNation. [SRC-003]
- A senior promoter reportedly described HyperVerse and HyperNation as one big entity. [SRC-003]

The exact legal and operational relationship between the brands is not fully established by the available evidence.

# Final OSINT Report: HyperFund / HyperVerse Alleged Crypto Fraud Network

## Executive summary

The benchmark evidence describes HyperFund and its successor brands—HyperVerse and HyperNation—as an alleged global cryptocurrency investment fraud network that combined:

1. **A pyramid/MLM recruitment structure** based on referral commissions and downlines.
2. **Ponzi-like economics**, allegedly promising very high daily returns without a legitimate revenue source.
3. **Public-facing promoters**, particularly Brenda Chunga, who marketed passive income, referral rewards, and apparent wealth.
4. **Repeated rebranding**, from HyperFund to HyperVerse and then HyperNation, while the underlying ecosystem allegedly continued.
5. **Credibility signaling**, including references to founders’ media exposure, corporate affiliations, blockchain expertise, and celebrity endorsements.
6. **A questionable CEO persona**, Steven Reece Lewis, whose claimed education and employment history could not be independently verified by the Guardian.
7. **Withdrawal restrictions and internal-token mechanics**, allegedly making it difficult for investors to convert nominal balances into usable funds.

The SEC complaint alleges that the network raised more than **$1.7 billion**, while DOJ materials and CNBC described the alleged criminal scheme as approximately **$1.89–$1.9 billion**. These figures should be treated as allegations or reported estimates, not as an adjudicated finding in this report. [SRC-004] [SRC-001] [SRC-002]

The DOJ expressly states that criminal charges are allegations and that defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty. [SRC-002]

---

## 1. Network identity and chronology

### HyperFund’s stated structure

The SEC complaint alleges that HyperTech Group launched HyperFund in June 2020 as a purported decentralized-finance ecosystem. HyperFund was later rebranded as HyperVerse around December 2021 and as HyperNation around May 2022. [SRC-004]

The DOJ identifies HyperFund as also being known as HyperTech, HyperCapital, HyperVerse, and HyperNation. [SRC-002] CNBC likewise reports that the project operated under these names. [SRC-001]

### Rebranding sequence

The evidence supports the following sequence:

- **HyperCapital**: identified as an earlier related project or name. [SRC-004] [SRC-002]
- **HyperFund**: launched in June 2020. [SRC-004]
- **HyperVerse**: rebranding around December 2021. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]
- **HyperNation**: rebranding or successor branding around May 2022. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

The SEC complaint alleges that these were successive iterations of the same project ecosystem. The Guardian reports that a senior promoter described HyperVerse and HyperNation as “one big entity,” although this characterization came from the promoter and should not be treated as an independently established corporate fact. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

---

## 2. Alleged investment and Ponzi mechanics

### Promised returns

According to the SEC complaint and DOJ case materials, HyperFund memberships allegedly promised passive returns of approximately **0.5% to 1% per day**, with investors told that their initial investment could double or triple. [SRC-004] [SRC-002]

The Guardian reports that HyperVerse memberships promised a **300% return over 600 days**, with a minimum membership amount of approximately **$300**. [SRC-003]

These promised returns were presented as arising at least partly from cryptocurrency mining operations. However, the SEC alleges that HyperFund had no legitimate revenue source and did not conduct the claimed large-scale mining. [SRC-004] The DOJ similarly alleges that the mining operations used to justify the returns did not exist. [SRC-001] [SRC-002]

### Alleged Ponzi operation

The SEC complaint characterizes HyperFund as both a pyramid and Ponzi scheme. It alleges that:

- There was no apparent legitimate source of revenue.
- The promised returns lacked a valid economic basis.
- Investor withdrawals were paid using deposits from newer investors.
- The scheme collapsed when withdrawals became unavailable. [SRC-004]

The DOJ alleges that investor withdrawals began to be blocked in or around July 2021, while the SEC complaint describes the broader collapse as occurring in 2022. [SRC-001] [SRC-002] [SRC-004]

This is consistent with a possible liquidity-driven failure: high promised returns created continuing obligations, while recruitment and new deposits were needed to sustain the system. That is an assessment based on the alleged mechanics, not an independent finding of fact.

### Internal accounting and withdrawal friction

The SEC complaint alleges that investors purchased memberships using Tether/USDT and received an internal balance denominated in **HyperUnits**. Withdrawals allegedly required conversion of HyperUnits into the MOF crypto asset and movement through the HOO Exchange before conversion into other assets or fiat currency. [SRC-004]

The complaint further alleges that HyperUnits appeared to be valued at $1 when deposited but were not necessarily convertible at that value on withdrawal. It states that MOF’s price had fallen to a very low level by September 2023. [SRC-004]

This structure could have served two functions:

- Making advertised account balances appear stable or dollar-denominated.
- Introducing conversion steps, market-price exposure, and friction that made withdrawals more difficult or less valuable.

That interpretation is an assessment of the reported mechanism; the source does not by itself establish that every investor experienced the same loss or withdrawal outcome.

---

## 3. Recruitment and MLM mechanics

### Referral-based compensation

The SEC alleges that HyperFund used a pyramid-style referral system to reward existing members for recruiting new investors. [SRC-004]

Reported mechanisms included:

- Referral commissions for bringing in new members.
- Additional rewards based on the activity of recruits’ recruits.
- Downline payments extending to as many as 20 levels.
- Community, VIP, and global rewards for successful recruiters. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

The Guardian describes a sliding-scale referral system and commissions based on recruitment down to 20 levels. [SRC-003]

This structure aligned the financial interests of existing members with continued recruitment. It also gave promoters a reason to emphasize recruitment and reinvestment rather than withdrawals.

### Reinvestment incentives

The SEC complaint alleges that promoters encouraged investors to reinvest rewards through “rebuys” instead of withdrawing them. [SRC-004]

The Guardian similarly reports that members were encouraged to reinvest earnings and receive additional HyperUnits when funds were not withdrawn. [SRC-003]

This could have reduced immediate withdrawal pressure and helped retain nominal balances within the platform. It also potentially made the scheme appear to grow through account balances even when funds were not readily accessible.

### Promoter incentives and apparent wealth

Brenda Chunga, also known as “Bitcoin Beautee,” was identified by the SEC as one of HyperFund’s top promoters and a major figure in its U.S. promotional activity. [SRC-004]

The SEC alleges that:

- Chunga reached the highest promoter level within six months.
- That level reportedly required at least $5 million in new referred investments.
- She received more than $3.7 million from the platform and investors.
- She used earnings for extravagant personal expenses and to help recruit others by displaying the apparent wealth available through HyperFund. [SRC-004]

CNBC also reports that the SEC complaint said Chunga received more than $3.7 million and used her earnings to fund personal expenses and recruitment efforts. [SRC-001]

This illustrates a classic social-proof mechanism: visible promoter success can make extraordinary returns appear credible and can shift recruitment from an abstract investment proposition into an aspirational lifestyle pitch.

---

## 4. Public promoters and credibility signaling

### Brenda Chunga / “Bitcoin Beautee”

Chunga allegedly promoted the investment through online seminars and videos. The SEC complaint says her presentations emphasized:

- Daily passive rewards.
- The ability to earn without working.
- Accelerated rewards from recruiting others.
- The supposed credibility of the founders and related companies. [SRC-004]

Her messaging allegedly framed the investment as low-risk because the founders were publicly visible and supposedly had more to lose than gain by misappropriating investor funds. [SRC-004]

This was a credibility-transfer strategy: the apparent reputation of founders, companies, media appearances, and public profiles was used to reassure prospective investors about the safety of the platform.

### Rodney Burton / “Bitcoin Rodney”

The DOJ and CNBC identify Rodney Burton, also known as “Bitcoin Rodney,” as another HyperFund promoter. [SRC-001] [SRC-002]

The available benchmark material establishes his alleged promotional role and criminal charges, but does not provide comparable detail about his specific scripts, recruitment volume, or compensation. Those details remain uncertain on the present evidence.

### Celebrity messages

The Guardian reports that HyperVerse released promotional messages from:

- Steve Wozniak.
- Chuck Norris.
- Jim Norton.
- Lance Bass. [SRC-003]

The messages encouraged support for HyperVerse or its CEO and urged people to join. The Guardian notes that these individuals were available for hire through Cameo and that it was unclear how the messages were obtained. [SRC-003]

The Guardian also states that there was **no suggestion that these celebrities knew the details of HyperVerse’s business model**, and that their messages did not refer to money or investments. [SRC-003]

Accordingly, the evidence supports treating the celebrity appearances as **promotional credibility signals**, not as proof that the celebrities knowingly participated in fraud.

---

## 5. Rebranding as a continuity and repositioning mechanism

The rebranding pattern allowed the project to move through changing narratives:

- HyperFund was presented as a decentralized-finance and crypto investment ecosystem.
- HyperVerse was presented as a metaverse or virtual-world project.
- HyperNation used language involving decentralization, autonomy, a “new world order,” and universal basic income. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

The SEC complaint alleges that the changing names and themes were used to capitalize on contemporary buzzwords and market narratives. [SRC-004]

The Guardian reports that when HyperVerse members experienced withdrawal problems, some were encouraged to migrate to HyperNation. [SRC-003]

This suggests a potential reputational-reset mechanism: when one brand became associated with withdrawal problems or investor dissatisfaction, a new name and more expansive ideological narrative could be used to preserve recruitment momentum. This is an assessment inferred from the chronology and reported migration, not a proven statement of intent.

The evidence does not establish that every legal entity, operator, or participant behind each brand was identical. The SEC and DOJ treat the names as related project iterations, while the Guardian reports a promoter’s description of them as one entity. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-003]

## 6. The questionable CEO persona

### Presentation as CEO

The Guardian reports that Steven Reece Lewis was introduced as HyperVerse’s CEO during a December 2021 global launch event. Promotional material described him as:

- A University of Leeds graduate.
- A holder of a master’s degree from Cambridge.
- A former Goldman Sachs employee.
- The seller of a web-development company to Adobe.
- The founder of an IT start-up. [SRC-003]

The launch video reportedly presented him as a qualified executive recruited by HyperTech Group.

### Verification problems

The Guardian states that it found:

- No record of Steven Reece Lewis at the University of Leeds or University of Cambridge.
- No record under that name in UK Companies House records.
- No record at the U.S. SEC.
- No Adobe public filing showing acquisition of a company owned by him.
- No confirmation of employment at Goldman Sachs.
- No LinkedIn profile or meaningful internet presence outside HyperVerse promotional materials. [SRC-003]

The Guardian also reports that a Twitter account in his name was created shortly before the launch, promoted HyperVerse for approximately six months, and then became inactive. [SRC-003]

These findings do not independently prove that the person shown in the launch video was fictitious, nor do they establish who he actually was. They do establish that the claimed biography could not be corroborated by the organizations and public records checked by the Guardian.

### SEC allegation of an actor

The SEC complaint goes further, alleging that HyperFund “hired an actor to pretend to be the new CEO” when HyperVerse launched. [SRC-004]

That is an allegation in a civil complaint, not an adjudicated fact in this report. The Guardian’s inability to verify the stated credentials is consistent with the SEC’s allegation but does not independently prove it.

The Guardian reports that Steven Reece Lewis did not appear in the HyperNation launch video. Instead, masked figures called “Mr H” and “Miss N” were presented as official ambassadors. [SRC-003]

“Mr H” reportedly described himself as an “evangelist in the new world order,” while the presentation promoted decentralization, autonomy, and universal basic income. [SRC-003]

The progression from a credentialed-looking CEO to masked ambassadors may have reduced accountability and made the brand more persona-driven than institution-driven. This is an assessment based on the reported presentations.

The SEC complaint identifies Xue Samuel Lee, also known as Sam Lee, as a co-founder and central figure in HyperFund. It alleges that he maintained control throughout the project’s lifecycle and was prominently featured in promotional materials. [SRC-004]

6. **Withdrawal friction**: conversion through HyperUnits, MOF, and HOO Exchange created additional complexity and possible value loss. [SRC-004]
7. **Brand reset**: when the platform encountered withdrawal problems, the project moved through HyperVerse and HyperNation branding. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

# Final OSINT Report: HyperFund / HyperVerse Alleged Crypto Fraud Network

## Executive summary

The benchmark evidence describes HyperFund and its successor brands—HyperVerse and HyperNation—as an alleged global cryptocurrency investment fraud network that combined:

1. **A pyramid/MLM recruitment structure** based on referral commissions and downlines.
2. **Ponzi-like economics**, allegedly promising very high daily returns without a legitimate revenue source.
3. **Public-facing promoters**, particularly Brenda Chunga, who marketed passive income, referral rewards, and apparent wealth.
4. **Repeated rebranding**, from HyperFund to HyperVerse and then HyperNation, while the underlying ecosystem allegedly continued.
5. **Credibility signaling**, including references to founders’ media exposure, corporate affiliations, blockchain expertise, and celebrity endorsements.
6. **A questionable CEO persona**, Steven Reece Lewis, whose claimed education and employment history could not be independently verified by the Guardian.
7. **Withdrawal restrictions and internal-token mechanics**, allegedly making it difficult for investors to convert nominal balances into usable funds.

The SEC complaint alleges that the network raised more than **$1.7 billion**, while DOJ materials and CNBC described the alleged criminal scheme as approximately **$1.89–$1.9 billion**. These figures should be treated as allegations or reported estimates, not as an adjudicated finding in this report. [SRC-004] [SRC-001] [SRC-002]

The DOJ expressly states that criminal charges are allegations and that defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty. [SRC-002]

---

## 1. Network identity and chronology

### HyperFund’s stated structure

The SEC complaint alleges that HyperTech Group launched HyperFund in June 2020 as a purported decentralized-finance ecosystem. HyperFund was later rebranded as HyperVerse around December 2021 and as HyperNation around May 2022. [SRC-004]

The DOJ identifies HyperFund as also being known as HyperTech, HyperCapital, HyperVerse, and HyperNation. [SRC-002] CNBC likewise reports that the project operated under these names. [SRC-001]

### Rebranding sequence

The evidence supports the following sequence:

- **HyperCapital**: identified as an earlier related project or name. [SRC-004] [SRC-002]
- **HyperFund**: launched in June 2020. [SRC-004]
- **HyperVerse**: rebranding around December 2021. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]
- **HyperNation**: rebranding or successor branding around May 2022. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

The SEC complaint alleges that these were successive iterations of the same project ecosystem. The Guardian reports that a senior promoter described HyperVerse and HyperNation as “one big entity,” although this characterization came from the promoter and should not be treated as an independently established corporate fact. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

---

## 2. Alleged investment and Ponzi mechanics

### Promised returns

According to the SEC complaint and DOJ case materials, HyperFund memberships allegedly promised passive returns of approximately **0.5% to 1% per day**, with investors told that their initial investment could double or triple. [SRC-004] [SRC-002]

The Guardian reports that HyperVerse memberships promised a **300% return over 600 days**, with a minimum membership amount of approximately **$300**. [SRC-003]

These promised returns were presented as arising at least partly from cryptocurrency mining operations. However, the SEC alleges that HyperFund had no legitimate revenue source and did not conduct the claimed large-scale mining. [SRC-004] The DOJ similarly alleges that the mining operations used to justify the returns did not exist. [SRC-001] [SRC-002]

### Alleged Ponzi operation

The SEC complaint characterizes HyperFund as both a pyramid and Ponzi scheme. It alleges that:

- There was no apparent legitimate source of revenue.
- The promised returns lacked a valid economic basis.
- Investor withdrawals were paid using deposits from newer investors.
- The scheme collapsed when withdrawals became unavailable. [SRC-004]

The DOJ alleges that investor withdrawals began to be blocked in or around July 2021, while the SEC complaint describes the broader collapse as occurring in 2022. [SRC-001] [SRC-002] [SRC-004]

This is consistent with a possible liquidity-driven failure: high promised returns created continuing obligations, while recruitment and new deposits were needed to sustain the system. That is an assessment based on the alleged mechanics, not an independent finding of fact.

### Internal accounting and withdrawal friction

The SEC complaint alleges that investors purchased memberships using Tether/USDT and received an internal balance denominated in **HyperUnits**. Withdrawals allegedly required conversion of HyperUnits into the MOF crypto asset and movement through the HOO Exchange before conversion into other assets or fiat currency. [SRC-004]

The complaint further alleges that HyperUnits appeared to be valued at $1 when deposited but were not necessarily convertible at that value on withdrawal. It states that MOF’s price had fallen to a very low level by September 2023. [SRC-004]

This structure could have served two functions:

- Making advertised account balances appear stable or dollar-denominated.
- Introducing conversion steps, market-price exposure, and friction that made withdrawals more difficult or less valuable.

That interpretation is an assessment of the reported mechanism; the source does not by itself establish that every investor experienced the same loss or withdrawal outcome.

---

## 3. Recruitment and MLM mechanics

### Referral-based compensation

The SEC alleges that HyperFund used a pyramid-style referral system to reward existing members for recruiting new investors. [SRC-004]

Reported mechanisms included:

- Referral commissions for bringing in new members.
- Additional rewards based on the activity of recruits’ recruits.
- Downline payments extending to as many as 20 levels.
- Community, VIP, and global rewards for successful recruiters. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

The Guardian describes a sliding-scale referral system and commissions based on recruitment down to 20 levels. [SRC-003]

This structure aligned the financial interests of existing members with continued recruitment. It also gave promoters a reason to emphasize recruitment and reinvestment rather than withdrawals.

### Reinvestment incentives

The SEC complaint alleges that promoters encouraged investors to reinvest rewards through “rebuys” instead of withdrawing them. [SRC-004]

The Guardian similarly reports that members were encouraged to reinvest earnings and receive additional HyperUnits when funds were not withdrawn. [SRC-003]

This could have reduced immediate withdrawal pressure and helped retain nominal balances within the platform. It also potentially made the scheme appear to grow through account balances even when funds were not readily accessible.

### Promoter incentives and apparent wealth

Brenda Chunga, also known as “Bitcoin Beautee,” was identified by the SEC as one of HyperFund’s top promoters and a major figure in its U.S. promotional activity. [SRC-004]

The SEC alleges that:

- Chunga reached the highest promoter level within six months.
- That level reportedly required at least $5 million in new referred investments.
- She received more than $3.7 million from the platform and investors.
- She used earnings for extravagant personal expenses and to help recruit others by displaying the apparent wealth available through HyperFund. [SRC-004]

CNBC also reports that the SEC complaint said Chunga received more than $3.7 million and used her earnings to fund personal expenses and recruitment efforts. [SRC-001]

This illustrates a classic social-proof mechanism: visible promoter success can make extraordinary returns appear credible and can shift recruitment from an abstract investment proposition into an aspirational lifestyle pitch.

---

## 4. Public promoters and credibility signaling

### Brenda Chunga / “Bitcoin Beautee”

Chunga allegedly promoted the investment through online seminars and videos. The SEC complaint says her presentations emphasized:

- Daily passive rewards.
- The ability to earn without working.
- Accelerated rewards from recruiting others.
- The supposed credibility of the founders and related companies. [SRC-004]

Her messaging allegedly framed the investment as low-risk because the founders were publicly visible and supposedly had more to lose than gain by misappropriating investor funds. [SRC-004]

This was a credibility-transfer strategy: the apparent reputation of founders, companies, media appearances, and public profiles was used to reassure prospective investors about the safety of the platform.

### Rodney Burton / “Bitcoin Rodney”

The DOJ and CNBC identify Rodney Burton, also known as “Bitcoin Rodney,” as another HyperFund promoter. [SRC-001] [SRC-002]

The available benchmark material establishes his alleged promotional role and criminal charges, but does not provide comparable detail about his specific scripts, recruitment volume, or compensation. Those details remain uncertain on the present evidence.

### Celebrity messages

The Guardian reports that HyperVerse released promotional messages from:

- Steve Wozniak.
- Chuck Norris.
- Jim Norton.
- Lance Bass. [SRC-003]

The messages encouraged support for HyperVerse or its CEO and urged people to join. The Guardian notes that these individuals were available for hire through Cameo and that it was unclear how the messages were obtained. [SRC-003]

The Guardian also states that there was **no suggestion that these celebrities knew the details of HyperVerse’s business model**, and that their messages did not refer to money or investments. [SRC-003]

Accordingly, the evidence supports treating the celebrity appearances as **promotional credibility signals**, not as proof that the celebrities knowingly participated in fraud.

---

## 5. Rebranding as a continuity and repositioning mechanism

The rebranding pattern allowed the project to move through changing narratives:

- HyperFund was presented as a decentralized-finance and crypto investment ecosystem.
- HyperVerse was presented as a metaverse or virtual-world project.
- HyperNation used language involving decentralization, autonomy, a “new world order,” and universal basic income. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

The SEC complaint alleges that the changing names and themes were used to capitalize on contemporary buzzwords and market narratives. [SRC-004]

The Guardian reports that when HyperVerse members experienced withdrawal problems, some were encouraged to migrate to HyperNation. [SRC-003]

This suggests a potential reputational-reset mechanism: when one brand became associated with withdrawal problems or investor dissatisfaction, a new name and more expansive ideological narrative could be used to preserve recruitment momentum. This is an assessment inferred from the chronology and reported migration, not a proven statement of intent.

The evidence does not establish that every legal entity, operator, or participant behind each brand was identical. The SEC and DOJ treat the names as related project iterations, while the Guardian reports a promoter’s description of them as one entity. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-003]

---

## 6. The questionable CEO persona

### Presentation as CEO

The Guardian reports that Steven Reece Lewis was introduced as HyperVerse’s CEO during a December 2021 global launch event. Promotional material described him as:

- A University of Leeds graduate.
- A holder of a master’s degree from Cambridge.
- A former Goldman Sachs employee.
- The seller of a web-development company to Adobe.
- The founder of an IT start-up. [SRC-003]

The launch video reportedly presented him as a qualified executive recruited by HyperTech Group.

### Verification problems

The Guardian states that it found:

- No record of Steven Reece Lewis at the University of Leeds or University of Cambridge.
- No record under that name in UK Companies House records.
- No record at the U.S. SEC.
- No Adobe public filing showing acquisition of a company owned by him.
- No confirmation of employment at Goldman Sachs.
- No LinkedIn profile or meaningful internet presence outside HyperVerse promotional materials. [SRC-003]

The Guardian also reports that a Twitter account in his name was created shortly before the launch, promoted HyperVerse for approximately six months, and then became inactive. [SRC-003]

These findings do not independently prove that the person shown in the launch video was fictitious, nor do they establish who he actually was. They do establish that the claimed biography could not be corroborated by the organizations and public records checked by the Guardian.

### SEC allegation of an actor

The SEC complaint goes further, alleging that HyperFund “hired an actor to pretend to be the new CEO” when HyperVerse launched. [SRC-004]

That is an allegation in a civil complaint, not an adjudicated fact in this report. The Guardian’s inability to verify the stated credentials is consistent with the SEC’s allegation but does not independently prove it.

### Masked successor personas

The Guardian reports that Steven Reece Lewis did not appear in the HyperNation launch video. Instead, masked figures called “Mr H” and “Miss N” were presented as official ambassadors. [SRC-003]

“Mr H” reportedly described himself as an “evangelist in the new world order,” while the presentation promoted decentralization, autonomy, and universal basic income. [SRC-003]

The progression from a credentialed-looking CEO to masked ambassadors may have reduced accountability and made the brand more persona-driven than institution-driven. This is an assessment based on the reported presentations.

---

## 7. Central figures and legal status

### Sam Lee

The SEC complaint identifies Xue Samuel Lee, also known as Sam Lee, as a co-founder and central figure in HyperFund. It alleges that he maintained control throughout the project’s lifecycle and was prominently featured in promotional materials. [SRC-004]

The DOJ charged Lee with conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud in connection with the alleged scheme. [SRC-001] [SRC-002]

Lee denied that HyperVerse was a scam and disputed being its founder, according to the Guardian. [SRC-003] The SEC complaint, however, alleges that he co-founded and controlled HyperFund. [SRC-004]

### Brenda Chunga

Chunga, also known as Bitcoin Beautee, was identified as a top promoter. The DOJ reports that she pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud. [SRC-001] [SRC-002]

### Rodney Burton

Burton, also known as Bitcoin Rodney, was identified as a HyperFund promoter and was charged with offenses relating to an alleged unlicensed money-transmitting business. [SRC-001] [SRC-002]

The DOJ’s case page states that criminal charges are allegations and that defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty. [SRC-002]

---

## 8. Integrated assessment: how the recruitment system functioned

Based only on the benchmark evidence, the alleged system can be modeled as a reinforcing loop:

1. **Attractive promise**: memberships offered extraordinary passive daily returns. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]
2. **Technical justification**: returns were attributed to cryptocurrency mining and blockchain-related operations. [SRC-001] [SRC-002] [SRC-004]
3. **Social proof**: founders’ public profiles, media appearances, corporate claims, celebrity messages, and a purported CEO were used to establish legitimacy. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]
4. **Recruitment incentives**: members could earn additional rewards by recruiting others and building multilevel downlines. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]
5. **Reinvestment**: members were encouraged to leave rewards inside the system and purchase additional nominal units. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]
6. **Withdrawal friction**: conversion through HyperUnits, MOF, and HOO Exchange created additional complexity and possible value loss. [SRC-004]
7. **Brand reset**: when the platform encountered withdrawal problems, the project moved through HyperVerse and HyperNation branding. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]
8. **Liquidity failure**: according to the allegations, withdrawals were blocked and the system collapsed when it could no longer sustain investor demands. [SRC-001] [SRC-002] [SRC-004]

The overall assessment is that the alleged scheme combined the economic characteristics of a **high-return investment fraud** with the social distribution methods of a **multilevel marketing pyramid**, while using rebranding and credibility theater to preserve investor confidence.

---

## 9. Contradictions and unresolved issues

### Contradiction 1: Lee’s role

- The SEC alleges that Lee co-founded and centrally controlled HyperFund. [SRC-004]
- Lee denied that HyperVerse was a scam and disputed being its founder. [SRC-003]

This remains unresolved in the benchmark evidence.

### Contradiction 2: CEO authenticity

- HyperVerse presented Steven Reece Lewis as CEO with an extensive biography. [SRC-003]
- The Guardian found no corroborating records for the claimed qualifications or career history. [SRC-003]
- The SEC alleges that an actor was hired to pretend to be the new CEO. [SRC-004]

The actor allegation remains unproven in this report.

### Contradiction 3: Reported loss or fraud totals

- The SEC complaint alleges more than $1.7 billion raised. [SRC-004]
- DOJ/CNBC materials describe approximately $1.89–$1.9 billion. [SRC-001] [SRC-002]
- The Guardian cites a Chainalysis estimate of approximately $1.3 billion in consumer losses during 2022. [SRC-003]

These figures may refer to different measures—funds raised, alleged fraud amount, or estimated consumer losses—and should not be treated as directly interchangeable.

### Contradiction 4: HyperFund versus HyperNation continuity

- The SEC and DOJ identify HyperVerse and HyperNation as names associated with the same alleged network. [SRC-002] [SRC-004]
- Lee reportedly denied involvement in HyperNation. [SRC-003]
- A senior promoter reportedly described HyperVerse and HyperNation as one big entity. [SRC-003]

The exact legal and operational relationship between the brands is not fully established by the available evidence.

key_findings.question: What was the alleged economic model?
key_findings.answer: The SEC, DOJ, and CNBC describe memberships promising approximately 0.5% to 1% daily returns and doubling or tripling of principal, allegedly justified by cryptocurrency mining that did not exist or was not conducted at the claimed scale. The SEC alleges that withdrawals were funded by newer investor deposits.

key_findings.question: How did recruitment operate?
key_findings.answer: The alleged system rewarded members for recruiting new investors, building downlines, and generating community, VIP, and global rewards. Referral payments reportedly extended through as many as 20 levels.

key_findings.question: How did public promoters support recruitment?
key_findings.answer: Brenda Chunga was identified as a top promoter who emphasized passive income, accelerated rewards, recruitment, and founder credibility. The SEC alleges that she earned more than $3.7 million and used visible wealth to recruit additional investors.

key_findings.question: How were celebrity appearances used?
key_findings.answer: The Guardian reports that Steve Wozniak, Chuck Norris, Jim Norton, and Lance Bass released promotional messages supporting or encouraging people to join HyperVerse. The Guardian found no suggestion that they knew the business model or knowingly participated in fraud.

key_findings.question: What was the rebranding sequence?
key_findings.answer: The evidence supports a sequence from HyperFund to HyperVerse around December 2021 and then HyperNation around May 2022. HyperCapital and HyperTech are also identified as associated names.

key_findings.question: What evidence concerns the purported CEO Steven Reece Lewis?
key_findings.answer: Steven Reece Lewis was presented as HyperVerse CEO with an impressive biography, but the Guardian reported that universities, companies, public filings, and employment records did not corroborate the claimed credentials. The SEC separately alleges that an actor was hired to pretend to be the new CEO. The actor allegation remains unadjudicated here.

key_findings.question: What role did internal tokens and exchanges play?
key_findings.answer: The SEC alleges that memberships were represented internally as HyperUnits and that withdrawals required conversion through MOF and HOO Exchange. The complaint alleges that the withdrawal conversion was not reliably pegged to the original dollar value.

key_findings.question: What is the legal status of the principal allegations?
key_findings.answer: Sam Lee, Brenda Chunga, and Rodney Burton were charged in DOJ proceedings, and Chunga pleaded guilty according to DOJ and CNBC. The DOJ expressly states that criminal charges are allegations and that defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty.

Reported amounts differ: more than $1.7 billion in the SEC complaint, approximately $1.89-$1.9 billion in DOJ/CNBC reporting, and approximately $1.3 billion in a Guardian-reported Chainalysis estimate of consumer losses.
A promoter reportedly described HyperVerse and HyperNation as one big entity, while Lee reportedly denied involvement in HyperNation. The precise operational and legal continuity is unresolved.

Recruitment was financially embedded in the alleged business model rather than being incidental marketing.
Public credibility signals were used alongside recruitment incentives.
The purported CEO persona was a central credibility device, but its biography is uncertain and the SEC alleges it involved an actor.
The alleged withdrawal process introduced an additional technical and market-conversion layer between investor balances and usable funds.

claims.claim: The SEC alleges that HyperFund was a global crypto-asset multilevel-marketing pyramid and Ponzi scheme that raised more than $1.7 billion.
The DOJ alleges that HyperFund and related brands were involved in an approximately $1.89 billion cryptocurrency fraud scheme.
HyperFund allegedly promised 0.5% to 1% daily rewards and represented that returns came partly from large-scale cryptocurrency mining.
The SEC alleges that HyperFund lacked a legitimate revenue source, did not conduct the claimed large-scale mining, and used new investor deposits to fund withdrawals.
HyperFund was rebranded as HyperVerse and later HyperNation.
Brenda Chunga, also known as Bitcoin Beautee, was a top promoter and allegedly received more than $3.7 million.
Steven Reece Lewis was presented as HyperVerse CEO, but the Guardian could not verify the biographical credentials attributed to him.
The SEC alleges that HyperFund hired an actor to pretend to be the new CEO at the HyperVerse launch.
Celebrity messages from Steve Wozniak, Chuck Norris, Jim Norton, and Lance Bass were used to promote HyperVerse.
The evidence supports an assessment that the network combined high-return promises, referral incentives, credibility signaling, brand migration, and withdrawal friction to sustain recruitment.
